div.p: In thispapec we present a new synchronization strategy for real-time tasks executed in a distributed environment, This strategy makes the timing properties of the system predictable since one is able to determine analytically whether the timing requirements of a task set will be met, and ifnot, which task timing requirements will fail. Inparticulal; every task is allocated on a diferent node of a distributed system and can require the use of non-preemptable resources or access shared data. The proposed synchronization protocol is based on the on-demandparadigm where resources are assigned only when actually required so that the system never wastes unused assignments. Simple formulae for the worstcase determination of task blocking durations as well as for the schedulability analysis of a set of tasks are described. A schedulability analysis example is also presented that illustrates the concepts of scheduling and resource allocation of a set of time critical tasks.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: The term scheduling of real-time tasks actually refers to the concept of sequencing the use of any shared resource whose use involves meeting application time constraints [4].

Alternatively, real-time scheduling is defined as the ordering of the execution of the tasks such that their timing constraints are met and the consistency of resources is maintained [7]. Thus, the objective of any scheduling algorithm is to find a feasible schedule whenever one exists for a given set oftasks such that each completes its computation before its deadline, and a given set of resource requirements is satisfied. We have to emphasize here that the CPU scheduling is not the main problem of real-time systems but both CPU scheduling and resource allocation.

In the past, hand-crafted techniques were used to insure the timing correcteness; however, these ad-hoc approaches resulted in systems which were not only expensive to develop, but also extremely difficult and costly to upgrade and maintain. On the contrary, an algorithmic-based scheduling methodology allows the developer to combine task characterization data with its associated timing requirements to determine through the use of formulae whether or not the task set is schedulable. This capability readily lends itself to automation allowing the system developer not only to quickly determine the timing correctness of current processing requirements, but also to be able to assess the timing impact of future system upgrades and modifications. The scheduling theory makes the timing properties of the system predictable. This means that one is able to determine analytically whether the timing requirements of a task set will be met, and if not, which task timing requirements will fail In current implementation practice, there have traditionally been two basic approaches to the overall design of application systems exhibiting real-time deadlines: the cyclic executive (also called a time-line) architecture, and the fixed priority architecture [4]. Some hybrid approaches are also investigated which are directed towards the development of suboptimal but practical algorithms that employ combinations of computationally simple heuristics [ 13, 7, 141. Interesting scheduling algorithms based on the cyclic approach can be found in [2,12,11,101 applied not only to single-processor but also to multi-processor environments.

In this paper, we present a new synchronization strategy for real-time tasks executed in a distributed environment, where each task is allocated on a different node of a distributed system and can require the use of non-preemptable resources or access shared data. Thus, we focus mainly on the resource allocation part of the scheduling process. The proposed strategy is analyzable and understandable at a high level, meaning that given a set of tasks we know in advance if they will meet their deadlines or not. It is based on the rate monotonic algorithm [3] in the way the priorities are assigned to tasks, and which also effectively creates an integrated resource allocation model. Thus, we consider our work as a fixed priority architecture based upon the rate-monotonic scheduling, which is the optimal static priority scheduling algorithm with good performance, low 131. complexity and minimal implementation overhead. The proposed synchronization protocol, called Set Based Syn- chronization Protocol, is based on the ondemand paradigm where resources are assigned only when actually required so that the system never wastes an assignment that will not be used. The penalty paid for this, found also in all the ondemand approaches, is blocking. If the blocking time is nondeterministic then the whole system becomes unpredictable and difficult to analyze. In real-time environments, the blocking has to be deterministic and for this reason our approach imposes a specific structure on this blocking to bound the blocking time. This enables us to have nice analysis properties and a high degree of system predictability.

The most well known synchronization protocol used by the rate monotonic algorithmis that of priority ceiling protocol described in [9,6] where the blocking time is deterministic and bounded. It has many advantages in the uniprocessor environment but its multiprocessor extension, i.e. the distributed priority ceiling protocol [6] is complex enough and requires also the remote procedure call to be supported by the underlying software. In our approach, we try to minimize the implementation requirements and the complexity of the scheduling and the synchronization strategy in order to have a more efficient scheme that fits well in the distributed environment. Our major objective in the proposed synchronization protocol concerning the task blocking time which is also the same objective in the analysis of the priority ceiling protocol described in [6], is represented by the following two sub-goals:
1. the worst case blocking duration of a task should be a function of critical section durations only.
to minimize the impact of blocking time whenever possible by letting a lower priority task rather than a higher priority task experience blocking.

As it is previously stated, the scheduling strategy that includes the proposed synchonization mechanism is based on the rate monotonic scheduling algorithm in that the fixed prioritiesof the tasks are assigned inversely to tasks periods.

Hence, task ti with period Z receives higher priority than t j with period T j if ?I: < Tj . In order to satisfy our second goal we would let, whenever possible, a lower priority task wait for a higher priority task, even if the lower priority task has been waiting for a longer duration. Given a blocking duration B of a task r with period T , then the ratio BIT is a measure of schedulability loss due to blocking. In our approach, as we'll see in the following sections, we try to minimize this ratio as much as possible.

div.head: Assumptions and Notation
div.p: Loosely coupled, time-critical distributed systems are used to control physical processes in complex applications.

Most tasks in such systems have strict execution deadlines, and depending on the strictness of these deadlines, tasks are categorized as either critical or essential. If missing a task's deadline is catastrophic, then the task's deadline is considered to be hard, and the task is categorized as critical. On the other hand, if missing a task's deadline is not catastrophic, then the task is categorized as essential [l]. In this paper, we consider only hard dealines for critical tasks where also these tasks can require the use of non-preemptable resources or access shared data. To guarantee that critical tasks will never miss their deadlines, they are treated as periodic processes, where the period of the process is related to the maximum frequency with which the execution of this process is requested. We assume that critical tasks are assigned priorities according to the rate-monotonic scheduling algorithmand static bindingoftasks to processors is used. Tasks are periodic, are ready at the start of each period, have deadlines at the end of the period and have known, deterministic worst-case execution times. Every periodic task is allocated on a different processorhde of the distributed system and can require the use of non-preemptable resources or access shared data. More precisely, CPU scheduling is not the main problem, but since tasks are inter-dependent the main problem is task synchronization and resource allocation. Hence, blocking due to synchronization has to be deterministic in order to have nice analysis properties and a high degree of system predictability.

We assume that every task asks for all of its global resources only once in its period and subsequently can release these resources ( one by one or all at once ) after their use. Two operations are used for this reason, taking as an argu- ment a set of resources: During task execution and within every period of the task, only one call of the allocate function can be made but many release calls may be made. The section between the allocate and the last release call constitutes the critical section of the task.

div.head: Conclusions
div.p: In this paper, we have presented a fixed priority scheduling mechanism with an integrated resource allocation model that it is analyzable and understandable at a high leve1,meaning that given a set of tasks we know in advance if they will meet their deadlines or not. This scheduling strategy has been designed for real-time applications that need a distributed computing environment where every real-time task is allocated on a different node or processor and can require the use of global resources. The proposed synchronization protocol places an upper bound on the task blocking duration and once the blocking durations have been computed Theorem 3.2 can be used to determine the schedulability of a set of tasks.

It is important to note that the proposed strategy can be easily implemented especially on a distributed system since only the message passing scheme is required to be supported by the underlying software. More precisely, when a task ri executes the allocate(&) statement requiring to enter into its critical section, an appropriate message is directed to the resource manager. This manager gives to ri the permission to enter, when all the resources in Ri have been allocated to ri according to the resource assignment strategy described in previous sections. The task ri then enters into its critical section, always remaining on the host processor. In the contrary, the most well known fixed priority scheduling strategy, the Rate Monotonic with Priority Ceiling [6] requires also the remote procedure call model to be supported since some real-time tasks must execute their critical sections on a different processor than the host. Tasks are statically bound to their host processors but athread of execution for each global critical section is created on the synchronization processor, which is different from the host processor. Such costly operations like the remote procedure calls are not required from the proposed mechanism resulting to a very efficient and simple method for synchronization and scheduling of a set of time critical tasks.

A prototype of the scheduling mechanism is under development on a distributed memory parallel machine with 5 12 processing units running the Parix [5] operating system. For future work, we will explore ways to find less pessimistic formulae and more intelligent techniques for a better evduation of the task blocking times. We'll also study the non-periodic task scheduling concept and its introduction in our basic scheduling strategy.
